title: Why food is the whole story of Indian inflation
standfirst: In India, inflation is food inflation. With food making up over a third of the CPI basket, any spike in onion or tomato prices can set the entire country's cost of living on fire—and hit the poorest hardest.
bottomLine: For most Indians, the felt cost of living is what they pay for food; the headline number that economists watch often obscures this, because a repo rate hike can't grow an onion.
body:
On a Tuesday morning at Azadpur mandi, a sabziwala is staring at a pile of onions that cost him ₹40 a kilo wholesale. Three months ago they were ₹15. The retail price in his shop has spiralled to ₹60. A kilometre away, a Zomato delivery rider is earning the same ₹200 per trip he made last monsoon, but now his own kitchen is burning a bigger hole in his pocket. Food is the inflation that India actually feels.

## Why does food bulk so large in India's inflation basket?

In a rich country, a household might spend 10–15% of its budget on food. In India, for decades, it has been nearly half. That is Engel's law in action: as people get richer, they spend a smaller *share* of their income on eating, even if the absolute amount rises. Because most Indian families are not rich, food still dominates the consumer price index.

In February 2026, India launched a new CPI series with base 2024, built on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey of 2023–24. The biggest headline: the weight of food and beverages fell from 45.86% (the old 2012 basket) to 36.75%. This is Engel's law unfolding in real time. Indians now spend more on services, housing, and data plans. But 36.75% is still enormous. In the same series, housing, water, electricity and fuels weigh 17.66%, transport and communication 12.41%, and health 6.1%. Food alone outweighs any other group by a mile.

### How the basket changed

| Category | 2012 weight | 2024 weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Food and beverages | 45.86% | 36.75% |
| Housing, water, electricity and fuels | 10.07% | 17.66% |
| Transport and communication | 8.59% (under Miscellaneous) | 12.41% |
| Health | 5.89% (under Miscellaneous) | 6.1% |
| Clothing and footwear | 6.53% | 6.38% |
| Restaurants and accommodation | – | 3.35% |
| Education | – | 3.33% |
| Recreation | – | 1.52% |
| Other (incl. pan, tobacco, intoxicants, household goods, etc.) | 28.32% | 12.5% (approx., derived) |

(Source: MoSPI, 2024 CPI series; 2012 series for comparison. The new basket has 358 items, up from 299, and now includes e-commerce, OTT subscriptions, and telecom data plans.)

In January 2026, the first reading under the new base put headline inflation at 2.75%. That looks calm. But underneath, food was swinging. Under the older 2012 series, which gives us a longer lens, consumer food price inflation was -2.7% in December 2025. That one month doesn't capture the full story—just three months earlier, it had been flirting with double digits. Food is never quiet for long.

## How heavily does food move the headline number?

Because food has such a big weight, its volatility can yank the overall CPI around. In December 2025 (old series), combined CPI inflation was 1.3%. Food and beverages contributed -0.85 percentage points to that figure. Remove food, and inflation excluding food that month was 4.3%. Core inflation (which also strips out fuel) was 4.6%. The cheap dal and tomato were masking a stiffer price environment in health, education, and services.

But when food goes the other way, it can add nearly two percentage points to the headline in a single month. A bad monsoon—like the one in 2015—and suddenly pulses jump 30%, vegetables double, and the RBI's carefully calibrated target of 4% with a 2% band looks like a joke. No other component has that power. Housing costs move slowly; transport is buffeted by global oil; education and health creep up. Food alone can lurch from deflation to double-digit inflation and back inside a year.

Under the 2012-based series, we can track exactly which foods are swinging. In December 2025:

| Food item | YoY inflation |
| --- | --- |
| Vegetables | -18.5% |
| Onion | -48.1% |
| Potato | -35.0% |
| Tomato | 14.4% |
| Pulses and products | -15.1% |
| Oils and fats | 6.8% |
| Mustard oil | 8.2% |
| Milk | 2.5% |

(Source: MoSPI, CPI 2012 series, December 2025)

Tomato, notoriously, can shoot up 200% in a bad month. The index for tomatoes stood at 259.6 in December 2025 (2012=100), meaning a kilo that cost ₹30 in 2012 was roughly ₹78. In September 2023, when tomato prices peaked, the index had crossed 300. The point is not the exact number; it is the swing. Food inflation in India is not a gentle upward drift—it is a series of explosions.

## What makes food prices so jumpy?

A Hindi phrase captures it: *baarish nahi hui toh sab mehenga ho jaayega* (if the rains don't come, everything will become expensive). India's food production, especially of vegetables, pulses, and oilseeds, is lashed to the monsoon. About half of the country's net sown area is rain-fed. When the monsoon fails, output collapses. For perishables like tomatoes and onions, there is little cold storage that works at scale. A glut in one season rots; a shortage the next sends prices through the roof.

The other driver is that Indians don't stop eating when prices rise. The demand for food is what economists call *inelastic*: you still need your daily roti, rice, dal, and onion. So a small supply shortfall creates a large price increase. This is pure supply-side dynamics. Money printing or loose credit might push up the price of gold or housing, but they do not cause a drought in Maharashtra.

Look at the indices for vegetables. In January 2014, the vegetable index (2012=100) was 124.6; by December 2025 it had reached 210.6. But that path was not smooth. It plunged and spiked with every harvest cycle. The onion index moved from 173.4 in January 2014 to 201.3 in December 2025, with breathtaking drops and leaps in between. Some of the worst spikes have followed unseasonal rains that damaged the kharif onion crop—exactly the kind of shock that no monetary policy committee can anticipate or prevent.

Pulses tell a similar story. India consumes about 23 million tonnes of pulses a year but produces only 18–19 million tonnes; the rest is imported. When global prices rise or the domestic monsoon is poor, arhar dal can quickly go from ₹120 a kilo to ₹200. Mustard oil, a kitchen staple across north and east India, saw inflation of 8.2% in December 2025 (old series) because of a poor mustard crop and high international vegetable oil prices.

## Why can't the RBI just fix it with interest rates?

When inflation rises, the Reserve Bank of India's textbook tool is to raise the repo rate—the rate at which it lends to banks. Higher rates make borrowing costlier, cool demand, and, in theory, pull down prices. But this works best when inflation is *demand-pull*: too much money chasing too few goods. Food inflation in India is overwhelmingly supply-push: not enough goods, period.

Raising the repo rate does not make onions grow. It does not mend a broken cold chain or repair a monsoon. What it does do is make the EMI on a home loan more expensive, slow down factory investment, and possibly threaten jobs. The RBI knows this. The dilemma is acute when food inflation is high and core inflation is also sticky. In December 2025, core inflation was 4.6%—above the midpoint of the RBI's comfort zone—even as food deflation kept the headline at 1.3%. If the RBI had raised rates to fight the core, it would have punished an already weakening economy while food prices were actually falling. If it cut rates to spur growth, it risked stoking future demand-pull when food inevitably turned up again.

The repo rate currently stands at 5.25%. In 2022 and 2023, when tomato and cereal prices surged, the RBI raised the repo rate from 4% to 6.5% over several meetings. Food inflation did not listen. By late 2024, the rate was lowered to 5.25% as growth faltered, while food inflation remained volatile. No central banker will publicly say interest rates are useless against food prices, but the minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee often reveal nervousness about the "supply-side" nature of the problem.

## Who gets hurt the most by food inflation?

Engel's law again: the poorer a household, the larger the share it spends on food. For the bottom 30% of the income distribution, food can claim more than half of monthly expenditure. For a salaried professional in Gurgaon, it might be 15%. So a 10% rise in food prices is a 5% effective budget shock to a poor family, but a 1.5% bump to a rich one. The cruelty is baked in.

Rural areas are especially vulnerable. Many rural households are net buyers of food: they may grow some wheat or paddy, but they buy vegetables, pulses, oil, and spices from the market. In December 2025, rural food inflation was -2.3% and urban -1.1% under the old series, but in a high-inflation month the rural number can be higher because rural diets rely more on cereals and pulses, which can spike sharply. In the onion crisis of late 2019, rural households were hit harder because onion forms a larger part of their thali.

The gender dimension is also stark. When food prices surge, women typically bear the burden of managing the household budget. They are the ones who reduce their own meals, skip the chai, or walk farther to find a cheaper vendor. The CPI basket does not measure that quiet suffering.

## Why are food prices political dynamite?

Governments in India treat food inflation not as a macroeconomic statistic but as an election emergency. The price of onion has toppled state governments—notably in Delhi and Madhya Pradesh in the 1990s and early 2000s—and has lost Lok Sabha seats for incumbents. That is why when onion prices cross a threshold, you see frantic policy: export bans, stock limits on traders, raids on hoarders, and import duties slashed to zero overnight.

The toolkit is crude but politically essential. The Food Corporation of India maintains buffer stocks of wheat and rice, procured at minimum support prices (MSP), which can be released to calm cereal inflation. For pulses and oilseeds, the government has a price stabilisation fund and sometimes imports directly. For onions, the standard playbook is to ban exports, impose stockholding limits, and sell from Nafed buffers at subsidised rates through Mother Dairy and Safal outlets.

These measures are often criticised by economists as distorting markets and hurting farmers. An export ban can crash farmgate prices even as retail prices remain elevated because middlemen hoard. But no political party wants to be the one that let onion prices soar and then faced angry voters at the next rally. The result is a constant cycle of knee-jerk intervention that creates uncertainty for farmers and traders alike.

## So what does food inflation really tell you?

Food inflation is the lived cost-of-living index for most Indians. The headline CPI can look serene—2.75% in January 2026 under the new base—while a family in Dharavi is paying 50% more for onions than last month and wondering what exactly the government is measuring. The official number smooths out extremes, weights items by average consumption, and assumes everyone buys the same things. In reality, your personal inflation depends on what you eat, where you shop, and whether you are rich or poor.

The gap between headline inflation and food inflation also reveals the true stress in the economy. When food deflation masks rising health and education costs, as it did in December 2025, the RBI may look at the low headline and think it has room to cut rates, while a household paying higher school fees and doctor's bills feels no relief. When food spikes, the RBI may feel compelled to hike, even though the hike will not cool the sabzi mandi. The result is a monetary policy that is constantly wrong-footed.

For the ordinary Indian, the lesson is simple: watch food. The headline number is an average; the price of your thali is the real number. And for policymakers, the lesson is harder: until India builds real cold chains, irrigation that does not depend on the monsoon, and futures markets that genuinely hedge risk, food inflation will remain the ungovernable heart of India's economy.

keyTerms.plainMeaning: Like spending less of your total budget on roti as you become richer—not because you eat less roti, but because you start spending on phones, fees, and electricity. This means poorer households feel a price hike in food far more than richer ones. It does NOT mean rich people spend less money on food in absolute amount; they usually spend more, just a smaller share of their total.

A basket of everyday things—dal, rent, petrol, tuition—tracked every month to see how much more (or less) you need to pay. It is a rough average, not your personal bill. It does NOT mean every household is actually paying exactly the index number; it's a representative sample.

Inflation after removing food and fuel, because they jump around too much to show the underlying trend. It's like looking at the price of a haircut or a hospital visit instead of tomato prices. It does NOT mean food and fuel don't matter; they just obscure the slow-moving inflation underneath.

The interest rate at which the RBI lends to banks, like a wholesale price for money. Raising it makes loans costlier to cool spending; lowering it makes loans cheaper to boost growth. It does NOT directly control the price of vegetables; it only nudges demand across the economy.

When prices rise because there simply aren't enough goods—like a failed monsoon cutting onion supply. Unlike demand-pull inflation (too many shoppers chasing too few goods), supply-side inflation can't be fixed by just raising interest rates. It does NOT mean the central bank is helpless; it just means its main tool is the wrong one for the job.

onTheGround.heading: Thik hai, but what does it mean for me?
onTheGround.body: When you see the news say 'inflation fell to 2.75%', don't assume your life got cheaper. Chances are, the dal you bought today cost more than last month. The official basket has changed: they now count OTT subscriptions and e-commerce purchases. But your biggest spend? Still roti, chawal, sabzi. The RBI raising the repo rate won't drop the price of your onions. So keep an eye on food prices—that's the inflation you actually feel. And if you're running a household on a tight budget, plan for the fact that onions will go berserk one month and crash the next. Nothing is ever steady in the sabzi mandi.

whatPeopleGetWrong: The biggest mistake: thinking that inflation is always about too much money chasing goods. In India, a bad monsoon can spike food prices overnight, and that has nothing to do with money supply. Raising interest rates can't make it rain.
caveat: CPI inflation is an average. Your personal inflation depends entirely on your own consumption basket. If you eat out often or live in a rented house in a city, your inflation experience differs from that of a farming family that grows its own food. The headline number smooths over those differences, so treat it as a rough guide, not your personal cost-of-living index.
